svg.aria-label: A decision tree. The question in the middle: if this is wrong, how cheap is it to undo, and what does it break before I do? To the left, the two-way door: an article, where a correction is a new version, or a narrow internal tool that can be switched off; there, use controls that do not get tired: a validator, a policy row enforced outside the model, a record read afterwards. To the right, the one-way door: an email in my name, or a tool that touches regulated data every day; there, put the person: sending in my name, typing a secret, spending money, deleting what has no backup.

To the right, the one-way door: an email in my name, or a tool that touches regulated data every day; there, put the person: sending in my name, typing a secret, spending money, deleting what has no backup.

text.tspan: CHAPTER 15 · DIRECTION IS THE SCARCE SKILL
How cheap is it to undo?
Not "do I trust the agent", which has no answer, but: if this is wrong, how cheap is it to undo, and what does it
break before I do?
cheap
not at all
If this is wrong, how cheap is it to undo?
and what does it break before I do?
A two-way door
An article: a correction is a new version, and the next reader gets the
fixed page. A narrow internal tool that can be switched off.
A one-way door
An email in my name. A tool that touches regulated data every day.
Use controls that do not get tired
a validator, a policy row enforced outside the model, a record read
afterwards
Put the person here
sending in my name, typing a secret, spending money, deleting what
has no backup
Why not a person everywhere: people approve almost everything they are shown; Anthropic measured that its coding agent's users approve 93% of
permission prompts.
Source: chapter 15, Direction is the scarce skill (v2.0.0-rc2), from the newsroom's How cheap is it to undo, and
Jeff Bezos's 2015 letter on one-way and two-way doors. The 93% is Anthropic's measurement, as the chapter
cites it.
